proposals.before: Emperor Xuan's taboo name was Yi; his courtesy name was Zhongda. He was a native of Xiaojing Ward in Wen County in the interior of Hedong, and his surname was Sima.
proposals.after: Emperor Xuan's taboo name was Yi; his courtesy name was Zhongda. He was a native of Xiaojing Ward in Wen County in Henei, and his surname was Sima.
proposals.reason: The source has 河內 (Henei), not Hedong (河東); the literal line misidentifies the commandery.

proposals.before: Cao Cao sent someone at night to test him in secret, but Sima Yi lay rigidly in bed and did not move.
proposals.after: Cao Cao sent someone at night to stab him secretly, but Sima Yi lay rigidly in bed and did not move.
proposals.reason: 密刺 is a secret stabbing, matching the literal field; 'test him in secret' omits the stab.

proposals.before: He stayed to hold Xuchang, was refeoffed marquis of Xiang township, promoted Protector of the Army with credential axe, led five thousand soldiers, and added duties as palace attendant and overseer of Secretariat business.
proposals.after: He stayed to hold Xuchang, was re-enfeoffed as marquis of Xiang township, promoted Protector of the Army with credential axe, led five thousand soldiers, and added duties as palace attendant and overseer of Secretariat business.
proposals.reason: Refeoffed is a corrupted spelling of re-enfeoffed and omits as required by the Chinese 改封.

proposals.before: The Emperor remained to guard Xuchang, was enfeoffed as marquis of Xiangxiang, became Protector of the Army with ceremonial axe, commanded five thousand troops, and was given concurrent posts as attendant within the palace and recorder of Secretariat affairs.
proposals.after: The Emperor remained to guard Xuchang, was enfeoffed as marquis of Xiang township, became Protector of the Army with ceremonial axe, commanded five thousand troops, and was given concurrent posts as attendant within the palace and recorder of Secretariat affairs.
proposals.reason: 向鄉侯 is Marquis of Xiang township; Xiangxiang fuses the place name 向鄉 into one word.

proposals.before: When the Son of Heaven returned from Guangling to Luoyang, he issued an edict the Emperor: “When I am east, the Protector of the Army shall oversee the west;
proposals.after: When the Son of Heaven returned from Guangling to Luoyang, he issued an edict to the Emperor: “When I am east, the Protector of the Army shall oversee the west;
proposals.reason: The literal English omits the preposition required by 詔帝曰, yielding an ungrammatical clause.

proposals.before: He resettled over seven thousand surviving households of Meng Da’s clan in Youzhou.
proposals.after: He resettled over seven thousand surviving households of Meng Da remnant followers in Youzhou.
proposals.reason: 餘眾 are remnant followers, not specifically Meng Da clan.

proposals.before: The court said: “Only you can shoulder the western front.”
proposals.after: The Son of Heaven said: “Only you can shoulder the western front.”
proposals.reason: 天子 is the Son of Heaven, not an impersonal court; the idiomatic rendering erases the named speaker.

proposals.before: So he moved west to Chang’an as commander for Yong and Liang, directing Zhang He, Fei Yao, Dai Ling, Guo Huai, and the rest against Zhuge Liang.
proposals.after: So the Son of Heaven sent the Emperor west to camp at Chang’an as commander for Yong and Liang, directing Zhang He, Fei Yao, Dai Ling, Guo Huai, and the rest against Zhuge Liang.
proposals.reason: 乃使帝 means the Son of Heaven dispatched him; the idiomatic sentence makes Sima Yi the unprompted mover.

proposals.before: Court opinion urged haste; orders told him to stay heavy-handed and watch.
proposals.after: Court opinion held that a distant expedition favored a quick battle; orders told him to remain cautious and wait for a shift.
proposals.reason: 持重 means remain steady/cautious, not heavy-handed; the idiomatic also inverts the court’s preference for a swift fight.

proposals.before: He demanded battle in a memorial; the emperor refused and posted Xin Pi with staff authority to leash him.
proposals.after: The Emperor angrily memorialized for a decisive battle; the Son of Heaven refused and posted Xin Pi with staff authority to restrain him.
proposals.reason: 帝 and 天子 are distinct actors; calling both emperor in one sentence reverses who petitions and who forbids.

proposals.before: Field commanders ignore distant edicts—if they could trap me they would not beg Luoyang for permission!”
proposals.after: Field commanders ignore distant edicts—if they could trap me they would not request battle from a thousand li away!”
proposals.reason: The Chinese has 千里而請戰, not the place-name Luoyang.

proposals.before: The sovereign rode to Ximing; Fu and Shi escorted him home to Wen with sacks of grain, silk rolls, oxen, and wine while every county clerk was told to turn out.
proposals.after: The imperial carriage escorted him out through the Ximing Gate; an edict ordered his younger brother Fu and son Shi to see him past Wen, awarding grain, silk, cattle, and wine, and commanded the prefects and agricultural directors downward to assemble.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English turns the send-off past Wen into an escort home and fuses the imperial gifts with Fu and Shi as if they brought them.

proposals.before: In ancient times, when three armies were outside, the general did not receive commands from the ruler.
proposals.after: The ancients said that even if the enemy has high ramparts, he cannot avoid fighting us if we attack what he must rescue.
proposals.reason: English substitutes an unrelated Sunzi maxim; Chinese is 敵雖高壘，不得不與我戰者，攻其所必救也.

proposals.before: In ancient times, when three armies were outside, the general did not receive commands from the ruler.
proposals.after: The ancients said that even if the enemy has high ramparts, he cannot avoid fighting us if we attack what he must rescue.
proposals.reason: Literal English matches the wrong maxim and does not translate 攻其所必救.

proposals.before: If the enemy can be defeated, then defeat him; if he cannot be defeated, then do not defeat him.
proposals.after: The enemy's main force is here, so their nest is empty.
proposals.reason: English is a different maxim; Chinese 賊大眾在此，則巢窟虛矣 describes the empty base at Xiangping.

proposals.before: If the enemy can be defeated, then defeat him; if he cannot be defeated, then do not defeat him.
proposals.after: The enemy's main force is here, so their nest is empty.
proposals.reason: Literal English does not render 賊大眾在此，則巢窟虛矣.

proposals.before: The face looked wrong—he woke uneasy.
proposals.after: Stooping to look, it differed from the ordinary, and his heart abhorred it.
proposals.reason: The Chinese 心惡之 records revulsion while looking in the dream; it does not say he woke.

proposals.before: Eunuchs led him to Jiafu’s bedchamber and the throne couch.
proposals.after: He was led into the inner chamber of Jiafu Hall and helped onto the imperial couch.
proposals.reason: The Chinese 引入 names no eunuchs; the idiomatic line invents that attendant class.

proposals.before: Palace attendants met him at Wan with imperial wine.
proposals.after: The Son of Heaven dispatched a palace attendant and a regular attendant to reward the army at Wan.
proposals.reason: 勞軍 means to comfort or reward the army; the Chinese does not mention wine.

proposals.before: At Shu Ke torched grain and ran.
proposals.after: The army halted at Shu; Ke burned his stores, abandoned the city, and fled.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic line fuses the place 舒 with the personal name 恪, yielding a nonexistent 'Shu Ke'.

proposals.before: [8] North Huai burst with bins; [9] colony troops stitched Shouyang to Luoyang.
proposals.after: [8] From then on granaries lined the region north of the Huai; [9] from Shouyang to the capital, agricultural officials and colony troops were linked.
proposals.reason: 京師 is the capital as such; the Chinese does not name Luoyang.

proposals.before: Year five spring: back from Huainan with imperial baton and wine.
proposals.after: In the first month of spring of the fifth year the Emperor returned from Huainan; the Son of Heaven sent an envoy bearing the staff of authority to reward the army.
proposals.reason: 使持節勞軍 does not mention wine; 'baton and wine' invents a toast.

proposals.before: Zhang Dang smuggled eleven palace women to Shuang’s revels.
proposals.after: Yellow Gate Zhang Dang secretly brought eleven palace talents including Shi Ying out of the inner court as entertainers for Cao Shuang.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English omits the named palace talent Shi Ying and Zhang Dang’s Yellow Gate office stated in the Chinese.

proposals.before: Li Sheng called before leaving for his province.
proposals.after: When the Governor of Henan, Li Sheng, was about to take up Jingzhou, he came to visit the emperor.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English drops the Henan governorship and the Jingzhou posting that the Chinese states.

proposals.before: Shuang bottled emperor south of Yi—palisade trees—few thousand men.
proposals.after: Shuang did not transmit the memorial, detained the imperial carriage overnight south of the Yi River, felled trees for palisades, and called several thousand garrison troops to defend.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic “bottled emperor” misidentifies 車駕, the Son of Heaven’s carriage, as if it were Sima Yi, and omits the untransmitted memorial.

proposals.before: Yanzhou’s Linghu Yu and Wang Ling turned traitor—raising Prince Biao of Chu.
proposals.after: The Inspector of Yanzhou, Linghu Yu, and Grand Commandant Wang Ling rebelled against the Emperor, plotting to install Prince Biao of Chu.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English omits Linghu Yu’s inspectorship and Wang Ling’s Grand Commandant office, which the Chinese supplies.

proposals.before: Marched Wang Ling east.
proposals.after: Thereupon he took Wang Ling back to the capital.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic invents an eastward march and omits 歸于京師, the return to the capital.

proposals.before: Wei Dan brought wine to Wuchi camp.
proposals.after: The Son of Heaven sent Palace Attendant Wei Dan with a staff of authority to reward the army at Wuchi.
proposals.reason: 持節勞軍 is a ceremonial army-reward mission, not bringing wine; 天子 and 侍中 are omitted.

proposals.before: Emperor returned from Gancheng—Son of Heaven again ordered concurrent Grand Herald Minister Coachman Yu Yi with insignia—promulgated appointing Emperor Minister of State—enfeoff Prince of Anping Commandery—grandsons and elder brother’s sons one each column marquis—income households fifty thousand cumulative—nineteen marquises total.
proposals.after: The Emperor returned from Gancheng. The Son of Heaven again ordered Yu Yi, concurrent Grand Herald and Minister Coachman, with a staff of authority, to appoint the Emperor Minister of State and enfeoff him as Duke of Anping Commandery; one grandson and one elder brother’s son each as a column marquis; food-fiefs totaling fifty thousand households; nineteen marquises in all.
proposals.reason: 封安平郡公 is a commandery dukedom, not a prince; 大鴻臚 and 太僕 are two offices.

proposals.before: Yan crowned him Emperor Xuan—Gaoyuan tomb—Gaozu temple.
proposals.after: When Emperor Wu accepted the abdication he raised the honorific Emperor Xuan; the mausoleum was Gaoyuan; the temple name was Gaozu.
proposals.reason: 武帝 is Emperor Wu of Jin, not ‘Yan’.

proposals.before: Liaodong butcher block.
proposals.after: When he pacified Gongsun Wenyi he carried out a great slaughter.
proposals.reason: The idiomatic line drops 公孫文懿 entirely and invents a Liaodong label not in this sentence.

proposals.before: Shuang feats—Yuan hundred days—Da ten—thought genius flawless.
proposals.after: Observe his inner heroic resolve and outer brilliant plans: he wiped out Gongsun in a hundred days and captured Meng Da within a full ten-day span; he thought his troop movements godlike and his stratagems in need of no second plan.
proposals.reason: The Chinese names Gongsun and Meng Da, not Shuang; ‘Shuang feats’ is invented.

proposals.before: Xin Pi gate—fake rage.
proposals.after: With the staff of authority he blocked the gate; his grand design was abruptly bent; requesting battle a thousand li, he feigned a wish to display might.
proposals.reason: 杖節當門 is blocking a gate with insignia, not the person Xin Pi.

proposals.before: He Chao Yīnyì.
proposals.after: Built a wooden palisade to fortify themselves. He Chao, Jinshu Phonetic Glosses.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English drops the lemma 為木柵以自固 and leaves only the commentator heading.

proposals.before: The line cites the Records of Wei alone—the standard abbreviation used below.
proposals.after: Commander of military affairs in Yong and Liang provinces. Based on Records of the Three Kingdoms, Wei zhi—hereafter cited only as Wei zhi, Shu zhi, or Wu zhi.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English omits the office being collated and the abbreviation scheme in the Chinese.

proposals.before: Liangzhou dated later decades.
proposals.after: Annals of the Prince of Chenliu: Liang province was established in the twelfth month of the fourth year of Jingyuan, more than thirty years later than this.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English omits the titled person, the Jingyuan date and month, and the stated interval.

proposals.before: Scholia: Zhang Yi records Fu Jian to Shu, brother to Wei—names diverge.
proposals.after: According to the Shu zhi biography of Zhang Yi and Huayang guozhi 7, the Jinshu names Fu Shuang and Qiang Duan as Wudu Di kings leading more than six thousand followers to surrender; those sources instead have Wudu Di king Fu Jian surrender to Shu while his younger brother led a host to Wei.
proposals.reason: Idiomatic English omits Fu Shuang, Qiang Duan, the surrender, and the cited titles present in the Chinese.
